## Sickle cell disease
Sickle cell disease (SCD), also simply called sickle cell, is a group of inherited hemoglobin-related blood disorders. Sickle cell disease is caused by an abnormality in the oxygen-carrying protein haemoglobin found in red blood cells. This leads to the red blood cells adopting an abnormal sickle-like shape under certain circumstances. With this shape, they cannot deform as they pass through capillaries, causing blockages.
Problems in sickle cell disease typically begin around 5 to 6 months of age. Several health problems may develop, such as attacks of pain (known as a sickle cell crisis) in joints, anaemia, swelling in the hands and feet, bacterial infections, dizziness and stroke. The probability of severe symptoms, including long-term pain, increases with age. Without treatment, people with sickle cell disease rarely reach adulthood, but with good healthcare, median life expectancy is between 58 and 66 years. All of the major organs are affected by sickle cell disease. The liver, heart, kidneys, lungs, gallbladder, eyes, bones, and joints can be damaged by abnormal sickle cells and their inability to flow through the small blood vessels.

## Gene therapy
Gene therapy is medical technology that aims to produce a therapeutic effect through the manipulation of gene expression or through altering the biological properties of living cells.
The first attempt at modifying human DNA was performed in 1980, by Martin Cline, but the first successful nuclear gene transfer in humans, approved by the National Institutes of Health, was performed in May 1989. The first therapeutic use of gene transfer as well as the first direct insertion of human DNA into the nuclear genome was performed by French Anderson in a trial starting in September 1990. Between 1989 and December 2018, over 2,900 clinical trials were conducted, with more than half of them in phase I. In 2003, Gendicine became the first gene therapy to receive regulatory approval. Since that time, further gene therapy drugs were approved, such as alipogene tiparvovec (2012), Strimvelis (2016), tisagenlecleucel (2017), voretigene neparvovec (2017), patisiran (2018), onasemnogene abeparvovec (2019), idecabtagene vicleucel (2021), nadofaragene firadenovec, valoctocogene roxaparvovec and etranacogene dezaparvovec (all 2022).

plan.title: How CRISPR Gene Editing Actually Works
plan.description: CRISPR began as a bacterial defense against viruses and became a tool that can cut DNA at a chosen spot. This video explains how Cas9 and guide RNA find their target, how the cell repairs the cut, an approved sickle cell therapy, and the debate over editing human genes.

beats.narration: One of the sharpest gene-editing tools ever made was not designed in a lab. It was found inside bacteria, where it has been fighting viruses for a very long time.

props.text: A gene-editing tool that came from bacteria fighting viruses

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.chapter: A bacterial immune system becomes a tool

beats.narration: Bacteria get infected too. Their attackers are viruses called phages, and a single phage can hijack a bacterium and turn it into a virus factory.

props.alt: Phages and bacteria under the microscope

beats.narration: But some bacteria survive and remember. After an attack, they cut a short snippet of the virus's DNA and store it in their own genome, like a wanted poster.
Those stored snippets sit between repeating stretches of DNA. Scientists named the whole region CRISPR: clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats.

props.definition: Clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats: repeating DNA with stored virus snippets between the repeats.

beats.narration: When the same virus returns, the bacterium copies the snippets into RNA. Each copy pairs with a protein called Cas9, which finds matching viral DNA and cuts it.
Then came the leap. Researchers realized the RNA could be swapped for a custom one, pointing Cas9 at any DNA sequence they chose.
Jennifer Doudna and Emmanuelle Charpentier showed this, and in 2020 they won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for developing this method of genome editing.

events.label: Doudna and Charpentier win Nobel Prize

beats.narration: Think of Cas9 as molecular scissors, and the guide RNA as a GPS address. That address is about twenty letters long, and it tells the scissors exactly where to go.
beats.chapter: How Cas9 finds its target and the cell repairs the cut

beats.narration: But how does it search billions of letters? Cas9 scans the DNA for a short tag called a PAM. Only beside a PAM does it stop and check.

props.definition: A short DNA sequence, NGG for the common Cas9, that must sit right next to the target site.
props.example: No PAM next door, no cut.

beats.narration: Next, it checks whether the neighboring letters match the guide. If they match, Cas9 unzips the DNA and cuts both strands. If not, it moves on.
Here is the surprise. CRISPR does not rewrite DNA. It only cuts. The actual editing is done by the cell, as it repairs the break.

props.text: CRISPR only cuts. The cell does the editing.

beats.narration: Route one is non-homologous end joining. The cell glues the broken ends back together, sloppily. Letters get lost or added, which often disables the gene.
Route two is homology-directed repair. Scientists supply a template, and the cell copies it. Broken DNA becomes a precise new sequence, a deliberate change.
So the recipe is: find, cut, repair. The guide RNA finds the spot. Cas9 cuts the DNA. The cell repairs. We choose where to cut; the cell decides how it heals.

props.heading: Find, cut, repair
items: Find: guide RNA picks the spot
Repair: the cell does the edit

beats.narration: In sickle cell disease, a flaw in hemoglobin bends red blood cells into crescents. They jam in tiny vessels, causing pain crises and damage to organs throughout the body.

props.alt: red blood cells moving through a vessel

beats.chapter: An approved therapy and the debate over editing humans

beats.narration: In December 2023, the FDA approved Casgevy, the first CRISPR-based therapy. Its full name is exagamglogene autotemcel. About 16,000 patients aged twelve and older were estimated to be eligible.
Doctors remove the patient's own blood stem cells. CRISPR edits them to switch off a gene called BCL11A, which silences fetal hemoglobin. Then the cells are returned to the body.
Fetal hemoglobin works fine, and it keeps cells from sickling. In trials, pain episodes were eliminated in almost all patients. But the process is complex, and access is limited.

Now the debate. Somatic editing, like this therapy, changes only the patient. Germline editing alters eggs, sperm or embryos, so changes pass to future generations. That is where the consequences become hard to predict.
In 2018, a researcher in China claimed to have edited human embryos that became babies. The outcry was wide. Many scientists said the problem was oversight: who regulates a tool this easy to use?

props.text: The question: who oversees a tool this easy to use?

beats.narration: Questions remain: safety, unintended off-target edits, fair access, and where treatment ends and enhancement begins. The takeaway: CRISPR can already heal, and how wisely we use it is our choice.

defects.quote: pain episodes were eliminated in almost all patients
defects.issue: Imprecise: trials reported that about 29 of 31 patients (roughly 94%) had no severe pain crises for at least 12 consecutive months. 'Eliminated' overstates it.

defects.quote: In December 2023, the FDA approved Casgevy, the first CRISPR-based therapy.
defects.issue: Omits beta thalassemia and the UK approval in November 2023. Also does not mention the cost, around $2.2 million.
A stat scene showing a date instead of a real quantity is weak; the 16,000 figure would suit it better.

defects.quote: Researchers realized the RNA could be swapped for a custom one
defects.issue: Skips the tracrRNA and the single-guide RNA fusion, and does not mention that the key finding was published in 2012 in Science.

defects.quote: how wisely we use it is our choice
defects.issue: A generic moralizing close that adds no concrete image.

missing: Name He Jiankui and give concrete details of the 2018 case

Cost and access barriers in numbers
Why HDR is inefficient in most cells
wrong_facts: 'pain episodes were eliminated in almost all patients' is loose; trial data show about 94% free of severe crises for 12 months.
judge.summary: A clear, accurate and well-ordered explainer that covers every requested element at about the right length. It is somewhat generic and thin on the ethics specifics (no named researcher, no cost or thalassemia detail).
